term: "Distributed Training"

## Simple explanation

Distributed training uses multiple accelerators or computers to train a
model. It can reduce training time or make it possible to train models
that do not fit on one device.

## Technical explanation

Common strategies include data parallelism, where devices process
different batches and synchronize gradients, and model or tensor
parallelism, where a model's parameters or operations are partitioned.
Communication overhead, synchronization, failure handling, and
reproducibility affect scaling efficiency.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Large datasets and models can exceed the compute or memory limits of one
device. Distributed methods enable larger workloads but add engineering
complexity and do not guarantee linear speedup.

## How it works

The training system assigns data, model components, or both across
workers. Workers compute forward and backward passes, exchange the
required gradients or activations, and coordinate updates. Checkpointing
and fault recovery help preserve progress.

## Practical example

In data parallel training, each GPU receives part of a global batch,
computes gradients, and synchronizes them before the optimizer applies an
update shared across replicas.

## Common misconceptions

- More devices do not always make training faster; communication and
  input pipelines can become bottlenecks.
- Distributed training is not the same as distributed inference.
- Reproducing a run can be harder when execution order and parallel
  operations are nondeterministic.
